label: copy-phase input p (fed-back p, recall_idx >= 2)
explanation: Token detector for the letter p fed back as input during the copy phase. All activation mass is on in_tok == p at copy-phase steps (phase 2); it never fires on any other token, never in the original phase or on <DEL>, and essentially never on the very first copy step (recall_idx 1, the p echoed right after <DEL>; ~0% of mass). About 15% of predicted steps stay inactive (mostly weak/threshold cases, e.g. p near the start of the copy). Magnitude: strongest examples are p mid-sequence (recall_idx ~3), and in a pp double the first p is roughly twice as strong as the second; activation rate is flat across recall_idx 2-8.

issues: Minor: precision is not uniform. It is lower at recall_idx==2 (0.735, the p input that is orig(1)) and for L==4 (0.71) than at recall_idx==3 (0.90). This is a soft trend, not a missing rule.

Minor: on the second p of a 'pp' pair (prev_tok==p), precision is 0.77 and the mass share (2.4%) is below the recall share (3.0%). On the first p of a pair (rel_tok(1)==p), precision is 0.999 and the mass share is 6.6% against a recall share of 3.1%. This confirms the explanation's untested 'first p is about 2x stronger' claim.

Claims verified on the test split: all mass is on copy-phase p inputs (in_tok profile: only p is active). At recall_idx==1, p has precision 0.003 and mass 0.0002, so it effectively never fires there. Every predicted step has in_first==0 and correct==1, so nothing is hidden there. Precision does not depend on in_count (0.85 for both 1 and >=2) or on to_go (0.81-0.87).
Test-split misses outside the predicate: 56 steps, 0.0% of mass, all weak first-copy-step p's. The false positives look like scattered weak cases with no token, length or history pattern.
